The maintainer raised the priority from P8 to P4 (2026-11-18). His words:

> the issues of using gpu shaders for different things should be prioritized..

The issue stays `needs-research`. An agent works the research in the research lane (no branch, no PR, no lane slot) and files the sub-issues. The agent sets each sub-issue to P4 while the maintainer's order stands.
claimed: coordinator research agent (Opus) · 2026-11-18T21:50Z · worktree/branch none · plan: research

## Research 1 of 4: method and literature

Sources are published literature and the CamCraft tree at `origin/main` `1613e42f9`. No vendor program, binary or output was used.

### The method

A raster nest replaces each polygon with a grid of cells. The grid is the "sheet raster". Each part, at each allowed rotation, also gets a raster. A placement is legal when no occupied cell of the part falls on an occupied cell of the sheet.

The literature names this method the "no-fit raster". It is the raster form of the no-fit polygon (NFP):

- Mundim, Andretta and de Queiroz, "A biased random key genetic algorithm for open dimension nesting problems using no-fit raster", Expert Systems with Applications 81 (2017) 358-371. The no-fit raster of a part is the set of grid positions where the part overlaps the occupied sheet.
- Sato, Martins, Gomes and Tsuzuki, "Raster penetration map applied to the irregular packing problem", EJOR 279(2) (2019) 657-671. Each grid position gets an overlap count (a "penetration"), not only a yes or no. Local search can then move parts out of small overlaps.
- Toledo, Carravilla, Ribeiro, Oliveira and Gomes, "The Dotted-Board Model: a new MIP model for nesting irregular shapes", Int. J. Production Economics 145(2) (2013) 478-487. Parts sit only on grid points. This is the same discretisation, solved exactly for small sets.
- Bennell and Oliveira, "The geometry of nesting problems: a tutorial", EJOR 2008. The tutorial compares the raster method with the NFP and the phi-function methods. The raster method is simple and robust, but its accuracy is the cell size.

The no-fit raster of a part is a correlation of two bitmaps: the sheet occupancy and the reflected part. This is a Minkowski sum in raster form. A fast Fourier transform (FFT) or a direct sum can compute it:

- Kavraki, "Computation of configuration-space obstacles using the fast Fourier transform", IEEE Trans. Robotics and Automation 11(3) (1995) 408-413.

The gap (kerf, tool radius, minimum web) is a dilation of the occupied cells by a disc. A distance transform gives each cell its distance to the nearest occupied cell. A part is then legal where each of its boundary cells has a distance of at least the gap:

- Serra, "Image Analysis and Mathematical Morphology", Academic Press 1982 (dilation and erosion).
- Felzenszwalb and Huttenlocher, "Distance transforms of sampled functions", Theory of Computing 8 (2012). An exact Euclidean distance transform in linear time.

### Where a GPU helps

The no-fit raster is the same small sum at each grid position. The positions do not depend on each other. That is a good fit for a compute shader: one invocation for each candidate position, an integer AND and a count.

I found no peer-reviewed paper that uses a GPU for irregular nesting. The method above is from the CPU literature. The GPU work is our own engineering on top of it. The tree already has one precedent for this pattern: `crates/ui/src/trace.rs` (lines 1-22) runs a compute kernel (`crates/ui/src/trace.wgsl`, `@compute` at line 190) with a CPU twin and a parity suite (`crates/ui/tests/trace_parity.rs`).

### Recommendation (taken)

Use the raster method **only as a first filter before the exact check**. The raster finds candidate positions fast. The exact vector check with `camcraft-geometry` (`geo2d::Region`, clipper2 on the 1-micron integer grid) gives the final verdict for each placed part. The NFP placer of #2158 stays the reference placer.

Dropped:
- "Use the raster as the only check": a cell has a size, and a bug in the rasteriser could pass an overlap. The Prime Directive needs an exact check.
- "Do not use the raster at all": the raster handles holes, remnants, keep-out zones and local search (#2164) with no extra geometry code. That value is real even without a GPU.

## Research 2 of 4: accuracy and speed

### Accuracy: can a raster keep a safe gap?

Yes, if the raster is conservative. Three rules make a raster result safe:

1. **Parts over-approximate.** First inflate the part by the spacing rules of #2158 (`cut_width + part_gap / 2` for an `Outside` cut, and so on). Then mark each cell that the inflated part touches, not only the cells that it covers.
2. **The sheet under-approximates.** Mark a sheet cell free only when the full cell is inside the usable sheet (sheet minus `edge_margin`, minus holes in a remnant, minus keep-out zones).
3. **Positions are grid steps.** A part moves in whole cells. Thus the occupied sets of the raster contain the true sets at each tested position.

If two over-approximated sets do not share a cell, the true sets do not touch. Thus a raster "free" result is a true "free" result. The cost is material: each part can lose up to one cell on each side. Two neighbours can be up to two cells further apart than necessary.

The exact check then removes the remaining risk. After each placement, `geo2d::Region` booleans test the inflated part against the placed parts and the usable sheet. A failure marks the part unplaced with a reason. It never passes silently. The exact check also guards against a bug in the rasteriser or in a GPU driver.

### Resolution for a 3 m sheet

| Sheet | Cell | Cells | 1 bit per cell | 1 byte per cell |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3000 x 1500 mm | 0.1 mm | 30000 x 15000 = 4.5e8 | 56 MB | 450 MB |
| 3000 x 1500 mm | 1 mm | 3000 x 1500 = 4.5e6 | 0.56 MB | 4.5 MB |
| 3000 x 1500 mm | 2 mm | 1500 x 750 = 1.1e6 | 0.14 MB | 1.1 MB |

A 0.1 mm raster of the full sheet is too large:
- 30000 cells is more than the wgpu 30 default `max_texture_dimension_2d` (8192).
- 56 MB is near the default `max_storage_buffer_binding_size` (128 MiB) and over the lower downlevel limits.

Recommendation (taken): **coarse to fine**.
1. Search the full sheet on a coarse grid (1 mm default, a parameter).
2. Refine each coarse candidate in a small window on a fine grid (0.1 mm), in tiles of 4096 x 4096 cells or less.
3. Run the exact vector check on the refined position.

Dropped: one fine raster of the full sheet (memory and device limits); a coarse raster only (it loses up to 2 mm of material for each gap).

### Speed: compare with the NFP method of #2158

These numbers are estimates from operation counts, not measurements. A benchmark sub-issue measures them on recorded fixtures before any GPU code.

- **NFP (#2158).** Each new part needs an NFP against each placed part and each rotation. Then a union of those NFPs. Burke et al. (Operations Research 2006) report seconds to minutes for the standard benchmark sets of tens to a few hundred parts. The cost grows with the number of placed parts and with the vertex count.
- **Raster.** Each new part and rotation needs one no-fit raster of the sheet. On a 1 mm grid of a 3 x 1.5 m sheet and a part of 100 x 100 cells, a direct correlation is about 4.5e6 x 1e4 = 4.5e10 integer operations. A bit-packed AND with a count reduces this by a factor of about 32.
  - CPU, one thread, bit-packed: about 1 s for each part and rotation. An FFT is about 0.1 s.
  - GPU compute: about 1-10 ms for each part and rotation.
- **Estimate for orthogonal rotations (4 for each part):**

| Parts | Evaluations | CPU raster (FFT) | GPU raster | NFP |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 50 | 200 | about 20 s | under 2 s | fast: few placed parts |
| 200 | 800 | about 80 s | about 1-8 s | NFP cost grows with placed parts |
| 1000 | 4000 | about 7 min | about 4-40 s | unknown: measure |

The raster cost does not grow with the number of placed parts or their vertex count. It grows with the sheet area and the part area in cells. A finer rotation set (15 degrees: 24 rotations) multiplies each row by 6. The largest gain is for the local search of #2164: each swap needs new evaluations, and the GPU makes many thousands of evaluations affordable.

Conclusion: the GPU gain is probable for 200 or more parts, for fine rotation steps and for local search. It is not probable for 50 parts with 4 rotations. The benchmark slice decides if the GPU slice continues.

## Research 3 of 4: platform, CPU fallback and determinism

### What the tree has today (`origin/main` `1613e42f9`)

- **wgpu version.** `Cargo.lock` has `wgpu` 30.0.1, `wgpu-core` 30.0.1, `wgpu-hal` 30.0.1 and `naga` 30.0.1, through `egui-wgpu` 0.36.2. No crate has a direct `wgpu` dependency. `Cargo.toml` lines 46-47 say why: `camcraft-ui` uses `egui_wgpu::wgpu`, so that the types match the renderer.
- **Who has the GPU.** Only `camcraft-ui` uses wgpu (`crates/ui/Cargo.toml` line 23). `camcraft-app` has no wgpu. The CLI and the MCP server are `crates/app/src/bin/camcraft-cli.rs`. Thus the MCP server and the CLI have no GPU path today.
- **Backends.** The window tries the native backend first: DX12 on Windows, Metal on macOS, Vulkan on Linux (`crates/ui/src/egui_app/gpu_select.rs` lines 97-113). The fallback chain then tries `Backends::PRIMARY` and `Backends::all()`, GL included (`crates/ui/src/egui_app/gpu.rs` lines 94-100).
- **A compute shader exists.** `crates/ui/src/trace.rs` builds a compute pipeline (line 127) and dispatches 8 x 8 workgroups (line 298). A device that refuses the kernel gives an `Err`, and the caller falls back to the CPU march (lines 19-22, 86, 142).
- **A headless GPU exists.** `crates/ui/src/headless_gpu.rs` (lines 1-102) requests a device with no surface. It tries the software adapter first (lavapipe or WARP, deterministic on CI), then the hardware adapter. With no adapter, a test prints a loud SKIP. `CAMCRAFT_REQUIRE_GPU=1` makes the SKIP a failure (lines 37, 81-101).
- **Browser (#31).** `crates/ui/src/egui_app/shell_web.rs` line 86 says the web build needs WebGPU or WebGL2. The blocking `device()` and the trace readback are native only (`headless_gpu.rs` lines 60-66, `trace.rs` lines 28-30).

### Which GPU path works on all platforms

Use a **wgpu compute shader in WGSL**, with integer storage buffers only. This works on DX12, Vulkan, Metal and browser WebGPU.

It does not work on WebGL2 and on old GL devices. WebGL2 (OpenGL ES 3.0) has no compute shaders. wgpu reports this as a missing `DownlevelFlags::COMPUTE_SHADERS`. The kernel must check that flag and the device limits before it builds.

Dropped: a render-pipeline method (draw the parts and read back an occlusion count). It also works on WebGL2. But it uses the float rasteriser of each driver, and that rasteriser is not the same on each driver. Determinism is more important than WebGL2 speed.

### No GPU: the CPU fallback (law)

**The CPU path is the reference. The GPU path is an accelerator with the same result.**

- The nest kernel lives in `camcraft-geometry` and evaluates the raster on the CPU. Headless tests, the CLI and the MCP server use this path. They need no GPU.
- The GPU evaluator is optional. It gives the same feasibility answer as the CPU evaluator, bit for bit. A parity test proves this, as `trace_parity.rs` does for the preview.
- When the GPU refuses (no adapter, no compute, a limit too small, a device loss, a validation error), the caller uses the CPU evaluator. The log names the reason. The nest result does not change.
- WebGL2 in the browser uses the CPU evaluator.

### Determinism (#2164)

GPU float results can differ between drivers. WGSL permits implementation-defined float behaviour, for example the flush of subnormal values and the accuracy of built-in functions. Integer arithmetic in WGSL has one defined result (two's-complement wrap). Thus:

1. **Rasterise on the CPU.** `camcraft-geometry` makes the bitmaps from the integer `geo2d` coordinates. The GPU receives only bits.
2. **Integer kernel only.** The shader does AND, `countOneBits` and integer adds. No float enters the decision.
3. **Order-free reduction.** The "first legal position" is the minimum of a packed key (row, then column, then rotation index). `atomicMin` on `u32` gives the same minimum for each order of execution. A scan on the CPU of the returned map gives the same result.
4. **Fixed budgets.** Each search uses evaluation counts, never a wall-clock limit (as #2164 says).
5. **Exact check last.** The vector check is in `camcraft-geometry` on the CPU, the same on each machine.

The result: the same input gives the same layout on each machine, with or without a GPU. There is no tolerance to state. A parity test on the software adapter and on any hardware adapter pins it. Dropped: "the same layout within a tolerance" (a nest that changes between machines changes the posted program).

The CPU reference also uses integer counts. An FFT correlation (float) is permitted only to order candidates. The integer count decides.

## Research 4 of 4: layer rule, dependencies and features

### Where the code lives

Recommendation (taken): **no new crate, no new dependency, no new crate edge.**

- `camcraft-geometry` (new module, for example `crates/geometry/src/nesting/raster/`): the conservative rasteriser, the bit-packed occupancy, the integer no-fit raster evaluation (CPU reference), the coarse-to-fine search and the exact vector check. It has no wgpu. It defines a small evaluator seam: a trait, or a function value that the caller passes in.
- `camcraft-ui` (new module, for example `crates/ui/src/nest_gpu.rs` and `nest_raster.wgsl`): the GPU evaluator behind that seam. It follows the `trace.rs` pattern: `egui_wgpu::wgpu`, error scopes, refuse with a reason, fall back to the CPU.
- `camcraft-app`: no change for the raster. The `RunNesting` command and its MCP tool of #2160 call the geometry kernel. The UI can pass its GPU evaluator in. The CLI and MCP use the CPU evaluator.

Why: `camcraft-ui` already depends on `camcraft-app`, which re-exports `camcraft-geometry`. Thus the GPU slice adds no `camcraft-*` edge and needs no decision entry for an edge. `wgpu` is already in the lock through `egui-wgpu`. Thus there is no new third-party dependency.

Dropped:
- A new crate `camcraft-gpu` with a direct `wgpu` dependency. It adds a crate edge from `camcraft-app` (a decision entry) and pulls wgpu into the CLI and MCP build. It gives no different result, because the CPU path is the reference.
- `wgpu` in `camcraft-geometry`. It breaks "one concern per subcrate" and makes each geometry build and test wait for wgpu.

If a later slice wants the GPU in the CLI, that needs its own decision entry and the owner's decision at review.

### Features

- **Grain (#2398).** Grain is a filter on the rotation set. The raster needs no change: it evaluates only the rotations that #2398 permits.
- **Vacuum zones (#2404).** A vacuum zone is a cost, not a wall. The raster can carry a second integer layer: a weight for each cell. The search then prefers positions where small parts sit on live zones. A clamp or keep-out zone is a wall: its cells are occupied in the sheet raster.
- **Holes that hold parts.** The raster handles this with no extra code. A hole of a placed part is free cells, and a small part can fit there. `allow_parts_in_holes` of #2158 clears or keeps those cells. The cut-order tree of #2159 then cuts the inner part first. The exact check confirms the clearance.
- **Remnant sheets (#2164, #2406).** An irregular sheet is a sheet raster with occupied cells outside its boundary. The rule "the sheet under-approximates" keeps each part inside.

### Fit with the open nesting issues

- #2156 (research): this research adds a candidate generator. It does not change the answers of #2156.
- #2158 (NFP and bottom-left fill): the reference placer and the input types. The raster slices use the input and spacing types of #2158. The held work is on `mkinney:issue/2158-nesting-kernel` and is not on `main`. The raster slices that need those types stack on that PR or wait for it.
- #2159 (cut-order tree): no overlap. The raster changes positions, not the cut order.
- #2160 (Nest entity and commands, blocked): no new command. `RunNesting` gets an optional evaluator choice in a later slice. The MCP tool of #2160 reports which evaluator ran.
- #2164 (local search and remnants): the main user of a fast evaluator. Its fixed evaluation budget stays.
- #1882 and #1884 (waterjet post and corner slowdown): no overlap. They act on the toolpath after the nest. The waterjet kerf enters the nest only through `cut_width` of #2158.

## Research complete

Recommendation: **use the GPU raster only as a first filter before the exact check.** The CPU raster is the reference. The GPU evaluator gives the same answer, bit for bit, and falls back to the CPU when it cannot run. The NFP placer of #2158 stays the reference placer. The research comments above give the evidence for each question.

Sub-issues, in slice order. Each is `P4` by the maintainer's order of 2026-11-18, and each is a sub-issue of this issue:

1. #2612 - conservative bit-packed rasteriser in `camcraft-geometry` (`effort:high`). Small and headless. Free to start now.
2. #2613 - integer no-fit raster search with the exact vector check, CPU reference (`effort:max`). Blocked by #2612 and #2158.
3. #2614 - benchmark against the NFP placer for 50, 200 and 1000 parts, with the go or no-go for the GPU (`effort:medium`). Blocked by #2613.
4. #2615 - WGSL compute evaluator in `camcraft-ui`, parity with the CPU (`effort:max`). Blocked by #2613 and #2614.
5. #2616 - browser: WebGPU with async readback, CPU on WebGL2 (`effort:high`). Blocked by #2615. Relates to #31.
6. #2617 - remnant sheets, keep-out zones and a vacuum weight layer (`effort:high`). Blocked by #2613. Relates to #2164, #2404, #2406.

No slice adds a crate edge or a third-party dependency. A slice that finds that it needs one stops for a decision entry and the owner's decision at review. No slice adds an MCP tool: the nest commands and their tools stay with #2160 and #2164.

Open item that this research cannot answer: the speed gain. The numbers in research comment 2 are estimates. #2614 measures them, and slice 4 starts only on "go".

Only the sub-issues are picked for code. This issue closes now.
